- When sentiment is positive (≥0.5) and forecast is trending upward, reduce slope slightly to avoid over-optimism.  
- If recent history shows sharp spikes followed by rapid decline, model should not overcorrect — maintain slight lag in downward momentum.  
- If forecast is flat or slowly rising but true outcome shows strong upward movement, consider sentiment-driven momentum bias — adjust upward by 2–5% of recent range.  
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast slope or cap upward movement to avoid “sentiment reversal” overshoot.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >10% from forecast in first 5–7 days, apply mean reversion correction: adjust forecast toward historical mean of last 10–15 days.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” values, model should not assume trend continuation — treat as neutral zone and forecast with minimal drift.  
- In high-sentiment periods (e.g., 1.00), if forecast is below true outcome by >5%, consider “sentiment lag” — forecast should be adjusted upward by 1–3% of recent volatility.  
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome in early days (e.g., 1–3 days), apply “early overshoot” correction: reduce first 3–5 days’ forecast by 2–5% to align with true momentum.
